content: Native copper, as a naturally occurring metallic element, is one of the few metals that can be found in its uncombined form as a natural mineral. However, it is more commonly found in oxidized states or combined with other elements. Historically, native copper was a significant source of copper and was utilized by prehistoric civilizations. Native copper can crystallize in rare isometric cubic and octahedral forms, but it is more frequently found as irregular masses or as fillings in fractures. When freshly exposed, it exhibits a copper-red color, but it typically weathers over time, developing a green tarnish composed of copper(II) carbonate. The Keweenaw Peninsula in Upper Michigan, known for its native copper deposits, was a major center of copper production during the 19th and early 20th centuries. These deposits are considered the largest native copper reserves in the world. Native Americans mined copper on a smaller scale, and isotopic analysis has provided evidence of extensive copper trading networks among indigenous peoples across North America. The first commercial copper mines in the Keweenaw Peninsula, often referred to as Copper Country, began operations in the 1840s. Isle Royale, located in western Lake Superior, was another site with significant native copper deposits. While some of this copper was extracted by indigenous peoples, only one of several commercial mining ventures on the island proved profitable. Another notable native copper deposit is located in Corocoro, Bolivia. The term copper itself is derived from the Greek word kyprios, referring to Cyprus, an island known for its copper mines since prehistoric times.
